tagline: Over Big Walker Mountain, above the tunnel and across the ridges
intro: Big Walker Mountain Scenic Byway crosses the mountain through Jefferson National Forest on State Highway 717 and US 52/21. The National Forest Scenic Byway runs 16.2 miles; America’s Scenic Byways suggests allowing about 30 minutes. Its account emphasizes overlooks across the Ridge and Valley landscape, with Mount Rogers visible from the mountain top. Interstate 77 passes beneath the mountain in a tunnel, while Route 52 crosses its crest. The byway account describes spring blooms of rhododendron, azalea and mountain laurel, with red and gold foliage in autumn.

The crossing also figures in the story of the 1863 Wytheville raid. Local legend credits Molly Tynes with riding through the mountains to warn Wytheville of approaching Union horsemen. The Union expedition targeted the Virginia & Tennessee Railroad and its telegraph line. The raiders occupied the town, but the railroad damage was repaired in less than an hour.

From the Bland end, follow US 52 to Big Walker Lookout at the crest. The 100-foot observation tower dates to 1947. Continuing toward Wytheville, the byway turns onto Route 717 and passes Stony Fork Campground. Here the road follows the east fork of Stony Creek through the Seven Sisters area before reaching the southern interstate connection.

moments.title: Bland
moments.text: Bland was first known as Bland Court House, a name that fits the reason its county was created. Residents faced long journeys and difficult mountain trails to conduct legal business at the existing county seats. They also objected to paying taxes for benefits outside their area. That pressure persuaded the General Assembly to create a new county in 1861 from parts of Wythe, Tazewell and Giles counties. Bland remains the county seat, in a county of mountains and small river valleys. The county took its name from Richard Bland, a Virginia statesman who served in the House of Burgesses and Continental Congress.

moments.title: Big Walker Lookout
moments.text: Big Walker Lookout adds a 100-foot observation tower to the mountain crest. Built in 1947, it has been operated continuously by the Kime family. The lookout’s listed elevation is 3,405 feet, and its view takes in mountain peaks in five states. The approach has changed: the original general store burned in 2003 and a replacement was built beside it. The swinging bridge once used to reach the tower survived the fire; it leads to the edge where the old staircase connected. Seasonal raptor migrations are another feature of the ridge: birds of prey use rising warm air from the valley to conserve energy.
moments.notice: The swinging bridge survived the fire that destroyed the original store.

moments.title: Wytheville
moments.text: Wytheville carried the name Evansham until a fire in March 1839, after which it was renamed. The Haller–Gibboney Rock House predates that change: its two-story limestone dwelling was built in 1822–1823. During the Civil War battle at Wytheville, the house served as a hospital. The building now houses a museum sponsored by the Wythe County Historical Society. Its late Federal design includes a side-gabled roof and a frame wing ending in a half-octagon. The Rock House belongs to the town’s historic district but has its own National Register listing, dating to 1972.
